title: Weak Values Beyond the Weak Limit: Measurement-Strength Invariance Under Post-Selection
abstract: Weak values are conventionally extracted in the limit of vanishing measurement strength. At finite strength, the corresponding post-selected conditional averages generally acquire nonlinear corrections and need not retain their weak value interpretation. Here we identify a class of measurement protocols for which this expectation fails: the conditional value reconstructed from the measuring probe is exactly independent of the probe strength and therefore coincides with the real part of the weak value. We first analyze this phenomenon in the measurement--disturbance protocol introduced by Lund and Wiseman. We then establish conditions under which this invariance persists, showing that it is determined by the interplay between the probe interaction, a subsequent measurement interaction with an ancillary apparatus, and the final post-selection. These results demonstrate that weak coupling, although generally sufficient for accessing weak values, is not always necessary.
summary: This work explores the conditions under which quantum measurements yield results independent of the measurement strength, a property called Measurement-Strength Invariance. The authors show that this invariance can be engineered in specific measurement protocols, allowing the recovery of weak-value physics without relying on the traditional weak-coupling approximation. This advances the operational understanding of weak measurements beyond simple theoretical limits.
main_problem: The paper investigates when the conditional expectation value derived from a quantum measurement protocol remains independent of the measurement strength, a property termed Measurement-Strength Invariance.
main_result: This invariance, which causes the finite-strength result to exactly match the weak value, is possible for specific measurement protocols, even when the weak coupling limit is not strictly necessary.
method: The authors analyze the measurement-disturbance protocol by comparing finite-strength conditional averages to the standard weak-value definition, generalizing the analysis from simple qubit models to higher dimensions.
model_or_system: The study uses the Lund-Wiseman measurement-disturbance protocol, analyzing quantum systems (qubits and higher dimensions) undergoing interaction with a probe and subsequent post-selection.

main_assumptions: The analysis focuses on the real part of the weak value and assumes the applicability of the measurement-disturbance framework.

paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the general failure of weak value interpretation at finite strength to demonstrating the specific conditions (interplay between probe interaction, ancillary measurement, and post-selection) that restore strength invariance, first in the Lund-Wiseman protocol and then generalizing to higher dimensions.
why_interesting: It provides a deep theoretical understanding of the operational limits of weak measurements, showing that accessing weak-value physics does not always require the idealized weak-coupling limit, which is crucial for designing realistic quantum measurement schemes.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Generalized schematic of the Lund–Wiseman measurement–disturbance protocol [11]. The system first interacts with a weakly-coupled probe through the unitary U probe A/B , which performs a weak measurement of either the ob- servable A (precision) or B (disturbance). The system sub- sequently interacts with the measurement apparatus through the unitary U app A . For the precision, the final readout is per- formed on the apparatus meter Mapp, whereas for the distur- bance the final readout is performed directly on the system in the B basis. Adapted from Ref. [11].

FIG. 2. Three-qubit implementation of the Lund–Wiseman precision protocol [11]. The system first interacts with the probe (P) through a CNOT gate, implementing a variable- strength probe of Z, and subsequently interacts with the mea- surement apparatus (MA) through a second CNOT gate. The probe and measurement apparatus are read out in the Z basis, yielding outcomes Zp and Zm, respectively. Figure adapted from Ref. [11].

FIG. 3. Three-qubit implementation of the Lund–Wiseman disturbance protocol [11]. The system first interacts with the probe (P), with Hadamard gates before and after the CNOT implementing a variable-strength probe of X. The system subsequently interacts with the measurement apparatus (MA) through a CNOT gate. The probe is read out in the Z basis, yielding Zp, while the final system state is measured in the X basis, yielding Xs. Figure adapted from Ref. [11].

FIG. 4. The system first interacts with the probe (P) through UP = exp(−igpOP ⊗pP), after which the conjugate pointer observable xP is read out. The system subsequently inter- acts with the measurement apparatus (MA) through UMA = exp(−igmOMA ⊗pMA). The probe statistics are then condi- tioned either on a final system measurement in the eigenbasis of OP or on an outcome xf of the MA pointer observable xMA, depending on the post-selection under consideration. The P and MA pointers are initially described by the position-space wavefunctions γ(x) and θ(x), respectively.
